slides.name: MonTi with two construction roles
slides.notes:
Planned speaker: Junyi Tang. This is a speaking plan, not a record of actual contribution or rehearsal.

Script:
This talk starts with MonTi, a model that constructs extra news articles and their connections to stress-test a fraud detector. We study a different construction workflow. A frozen upstream model commits the article features and target connections. A small downstream model then completes the connections to surrounding candidates. The question is whether this division of work helps under the same total budget. We will separate a completed development pilot from the registered full test.

Sources:
https://arxiv.org/html/2412.18370v3
https://github.com/TangWalden/CISC8006-MonTi/blob/70c48d1a74aa4e5b3e1b1c6ce15c068ba8931980/experiments/downstream_cooperation/README.md

Script:
A group is simply a list of target articles evaluated together. Here, the four orange circles are fake-news articles that the detector should identify. The outlined circles are surrounding candidate articles; they are not automatically benign. The square represents a new article that an attack may introduce. The attack does not get to replace the target list after seeing the outcome. This drawing explains the roles only; it is not an actual measured group.

slides.name: MonTi learns features and connections together

elements.html: MonTi learns features and connections together

One generator chooses new features
and target / candidate connections.
Schematic pipeline · graph connections are undirected

slides.notes:
Planned speaker: Junyi Tang. This is a speaking plan, not a record of actual contribution or rehearsal.

Script:
MonTi is a learned graph-injection attack. It reads representations of the target group and selected surrounding candidates, mixes this context with a Transformer, and generates features for new articles. It also scores possible connections. Those connections can lead to targets or to candidates. Training uses a surrogate detector to learn constructions that cause more fake targets to be missed. The original idea already combines several targets and coordinated injected nodes; our proposal changes how construction work is divided.

Sources:
https://arxiv.org/html/2412.18370v3
https://github.com/TangWalden/CISC8006-MonTi/blob/70c48d1a74aa4e5b3e1b1c6ce15c068ba8931980/experiments/downstream_cooperation/README.md

slides.name: Can a specialist complete a frozen MonTi plan?

elements.html:
Can a specialist complete
a frozen MonTi plan?

Commit the upstream plan.
Train only its completion.

slides.notes:
Planned speaker: Junyi Tang. This is a speaking plan, not a record of actual contribution or rehearsal.

Script:
The question is operational, rather than a claim about real criminal job roles. Instead of asking one generator to make every decision at once, can a specialist complete a plan that another model has already fixed? The upstream keeps its original weights. Its generated article features and the selected target connections become commitments. The downstream may choose only the remaining candidate connections. Both stages still use one shared node budget and one shared total edge budget.

Sources:
https://arxiv.org/html/2412.18370v3
https://github.com/TangWalden/CISC8006-MonTi/blob/70c48d1a74aa4e5b3e1b1c6ce15c068ba8931980/experiments/downstream_cooperation/README.md

slides.name: A fixed upstream and a trained downstream

elements.html: A fixed upstream and a trained downstream
Illustrative graph · a small specialist, not a second full MonTi

slides.notes:
Planned speaker: Junyi Tang. This is a speaking plan, not a record of actual contribution or rehearsal.

Script:
In this workflow, the upstream produces the new article features and scores the possible edges. We freeze those features and construct the target-edge block within the agreed quota. The downstream is a smaller scorer with 151,872 trainable parameters. It receives the frozen construction context and selects candidate connections for the remaining quota. It does not generate another set of articles, change the upstream weights, or add a second budget. The dark and orange lines show two construction roles, not directed graph edges.

Sources:
https://github.com/TangWalden/CISC8006-MonTi/blob/70c48d1a74aa4e5b3e1b1c6ce15c068ba8931980/experiments/downstream_cooperation/README.md

slides.name: The total budget stays fixed

elements.html: Aim for half. Project to the closest feasible split.
Illustrative 8-edge examples · unique edges · no injected-to-injected edges

slides.notes:
Planned speaker: Junyi Tang. This is a speaking plan, not a record of actual contribution or rehearsal.

Script:
The total structural node and edge budget is fixed, but a perfect half split is not always possible. In the first illustration, one new article has four available targets and at least four candidates, so eight edges can split four and four. In the second, only two targets are available. Duplicating a target edge is forbidden, so the same eight-edge budget becomes two target edges and six candidate edges. The actual algorithm chooses the closest feasible half split and reports the realized ratio.

slides.name: GCN teaches the downstream. GAGA tests transfer.

elements.html:
GCN teaches the downstream.
GAGA tests transfer.

Final weights and graphs are sealed
before GAGA evaluation.
GAGA supplies evaluation only, with no training feedback.

slides.notes:
Planned speaker: Yifan Fan. This is a speaking plan, not a record of actual contribution or rehearsal.

Script:
The downstream learns from a frozen GCN on the training groups. GCN supplies a differentiable training signal, while its own parameters stay unchanged. We train the downstream for four fixed epochs, then seal its final weights and the evaluation graphs. GAGA is a separate detector used to measure transfer after that commitment. There is no arrow back from GAGA: its evaluation outcomes do not train the scorer or select a checkpoint. This separation matters because learning and evaluation answer different questions.

Sources:
https://github.com/TangWalden/CISC8006-MonTi/blob/70c48d1a74aa4e5b3e1b1c6ce15c068ba8931980/experiments/downstream_cooperation/README.md

slides.name: Three methods share the same cases and budgets

elements.html: Three methods share the same cases and budgets
All three reuse the same upstream article features.
Same group list, node budget and total edge budget

slides.notes:
Planned speaker: Yifan Fan. This is a speaking plan, not a record of actual contribution or rehearsal.

Script:
The main comparison has three methods. Native MonTi keeps its own connection plan. The random completion control uses the same projected quotas and frozen target block as the staged method, but picks candidate connections randomly. The staged method learns those candidate choices. All three reuse the upstream article features and the same total node and edge budgets. The completed pilot additionally retained an original-score completion arm in its saved evidence. This table presents the three methods registered for the full test.

slides.name: The pilot improved miss rate over our MonTi baseline

elements.html:
The pilot improved miss rate
over our MonTi baseline
GAGA miss rate (%) · higher means more missed fraud
Completed development VALID pilot · 64 groups · seeds 3, 4, 5
Miss rate (MR) · click for an example ↗

slides.notes:
Planned speaker: Yifan Fan. This is a speaking plan, not a record of actual contribution or rehearsal.

Script:
These are the completed development results on the fixed GAGA detector. Higher miss rate means more fake target articles escape detection. Our native MonTi baseline averages 53.65 percent, the random candidate completion reaches 57.03 percent, and the trained staged pipeline reaches 58.14 percent. The staged gain over native is 4.50 percentage points. These are our own baseline weights on 64 validation groups per seed, not the paper table or the formal test. Click the miss-rate label for a concrete counting example.

slides.name: All three pilot seeds improved over native MonTi

elements.html:
All three pilot seeds improved
over native MonTi

Vs random: +1.11 pp
95% interval [-3.99, +6.21] pp
Still uncertain with three seeds.
Development VALID pilot · three paired training seeds

slides.notes:
Planned speaker: Yifan Fan. This is a speaking plan, not a record of actual contribution or rehearsal.

Script:
The three paired pilot gains over native MonTi are 6.13, 4.38, and 2.98 percentage points. Their mean is positive, and the nominal paired interval is above zero. The harder question is whether learning candidate connections helps beyond random completion. That average difference is 1.11 points, but its interval crosses zero and one seed is negative. We therefore have encouraging development evidence for the full staged workflow, while the learning-specific advantage remains uncertain in this small pilot.

The formal evaluation is registered separately from the development pilot. It uses 937 training groups, 909 test groups, and seeds zero, one, and two, with 10,515 target occurrences per seed. slides.name: Frozen upstream + trained downstream

elements.html:
A reusable MonTi planner
with a specialized edge policy

Development pilot: +4.50 pp over native.
Learning vs random remains uncertain.
Full-test results pending; the registered design is fixed.

slides.notes:
Planned speaker: Yifan Fan. This is a speaking plan, not a record of actual contribution or rehearsal.

Script:
Our proposal is a staged construction workflow: freeze an upstream MonTi plan, then train a smaller model to complete the candidate connections. It preserves the total attack budget and compares against both native MonTi and random completion. The development pilot supports further evaluation of the whole workflow, but does not settle whether learned completion reliably beats random choice. The report and repository retain the complete evidence, including less favorable controls. The registered full test remains a separate result, with its actual status stated explicitly.

slides.name: Miss rate: a four-target example

elements.html: All four articles are fake · total MR after attack = 50% · newly missed = 25%

slides.notes:
Planned speaker: Optional appendix; either presenter. This is a speaking plan, not a record of actual contribution or rehearsal.

Script:
All four target articles are fake in this illustrative group. Before the attack, one is already missed, so the clean miss rate is one out of four, or 25 percent. After the attack, two are missed, giving a total miss rate of 50 percent. Only one of those misses is new, so the newly missed proportion is 25 percent. The paper-style total miss-rate metric includes existing clean misses. We retain every target in the denominator rather than filtering to favorable cases.

Sources:
https://github.com/TangWalden/CISC8006-MonTi/blob/70c48d1a74aa4e5b3e1b1c6ce15c068ba8931980/results/downstream_cooperation/latest.json

slides.name: Quota rule and evidence sources

elements.html:
qT = clip(ceil(E / 2),
max(B, E − B·C), min(B·T, E))
qC = E − qT
B injected articles · T targets · C candidates · E total edges

1. MonTi paper — original method
2. Versioned pilot tables — measured development results
3. Frozen full-test protocol — registered comparison

slides.notes:
Planned speaker: Optional appendix; either presenter. This is a speaking plan, not a record of actual contribution or rehearsal.

Script:
The formula starts from half of the total edge budget, rounded toward targets. It then projects into a feasible interval. Each new article needs at least one target connection; the total available target and candidate pairs impose the other bounds. The remaining edges go to candidates, without duplicate pairs or extra injected-to-injected edges in the completion methods. Three source categories support this talk: the original paper, the versioned completed pilot evidence, and the frozen full-test registration. Exact links are recorded here.
